If you're wondering...

Do you really have to compost all your garden waste?

The compost bin often feels like the mandatory final destination for everything you pull out of the garden: spent plants, cut-back leaves, weeding scraps — all neatly collected, broken down, and brought back months later as dark soil. It's a good habit, but it's not the only one, and definitely not always the best one. A forest, after all, doesn't compost. The leaves that fall stay right where they fall, and the soil beneath is no less rich for it.

That "leave it in place" approach is called chop-and-drop: you cut or mow the material and simply let it lie as mulch right where it grew. The big advantage is that nothing gets lost along the way. A compost bin loses part of its nitrogen to the air during the rotting process, and you're also physically moving nutrients from one spot to another — taking them away from exactly where the plant built them up, and only bringing them back months later, diluted across the whole compost heap, somewhere else. Leaving material in place costs no labor, no time, and no loss: it immediately becomes food for the soil life again, exactly where it was needed.

Still, composting isn't pointless — it just has a few specific jobs. Material that's diseased — leaves with mildew, plants with root rot — is better off not simply left lying around, since that would spread exactly the fungus or bacteria you're trying to get rid of. A well-built, hot compost bin can render those pathogens harmless, along with weed seeds that would otherwise just germinate again right where you pulled them out. And there's one job chop-and-drop simply can't take over: good seed-starting and cutting soil isn't made with loose leaves or twigs on the ground, but with fine, fully matured, sieved compost. For raising seedlings and cuttings, you just need that refined, controlled material — there's no shortcut for that.

Composting is also a handy option when a lot of material suddenly becomes available at once — a mowing session, trimming a hedge — more than you can use as mulch in one go. But that doesn't have to go straight to the compost bin: a mulch holding pile is often a better alternative. Instead of letting that material break down into compost, you simply leave it as a stockpile — a separate heap of coarse material you draw from whenever you need fresh mulch somewhere. That way you lose nothing to the composting process, and you always have mulch on hand right away instead of only months later.

The rule of thumb, then, becomes: leave what's healthy where it already lies, keep a surplus as a mulch holding pile rather than composting it right away, and reserve the compost bin for what really needs it — diseased material, seed-bearing weeds, and the fine soil you need for seedlings and cuttings. So compost isn't a goal in itself, but it remains an indispensable tool for a few jobs chop-and-drop simply can't take over.

Composting isn't mandatory for everything, but it is indispensable for what chop-and-drop can't handle: diseased material, seed-bearing weeds, and fine seed-starting and cutting soil. For a sudden surplus, a mulch holding pile is often smarter than the compost bin.
